## Composing two networks

**Network 1**

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_1 &= a[\theta_{10}+\theta_{11}x]\\
h_2 &= a[\theta_{20}+\theta_{21}x]\\
h_3 &= a[\theta_{30}+\theta_{31}x]\\[2mm]
y &= \phi_0+\phi_1h_1+\phi_2h_2+\phi_3h_3
\end{aligned}
$$

**Network 2**

$$
\begin{aligned}
h'_1 &= a[\theta'_{10}+\theta'_{11}y]\\
h'_2 &= a[\theta'_{20}+\theta'_{21}y]\\
h'_3 &= a[\theta'_{30}+\theta'_{31}y]\\[2mm]
y' &= \phi'_0+\phi'_1h'_1+\phi'_2h'_2+\phi'_3h'_3
\end{aligned}
$$

## Combine two networks into one

The first network outputs $y$, which is the input to the second network.

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_i &= a[\theta_{i0}+\theta_{i1}x], && i=1,2,3\\
y &= \phi_0+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\phi_j h_j\\
h'_i &= a[\theta'_{i0}+\theta'_{i1}y], && i=1,2,3\\
y' &= \phi'_0+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\phi'_j h'_j
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the first output into the second hidden layer:

$$h'_i=a\!\left[\theta'_{i0}+\theta'_{i1}\phi_0+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\theta'_{i1}\phi_jh_j\right].$$

---

## Create new variables

Define

$$\psi_{i0}=\theta'_{i0}+\theta'_{i1}\phi_0, \qquad
\psi_{ij}=\theta'_{i1}\phi_j,\quad i,j=1,2,3.$$

Then the hidden units of the second network become

$$
\begin{aligned}
h'_1&=a[\psi_{10}+\psi_{11}h_1+\psi_{12}h_2+\psi_{13}h_3]\\
h'_2&=a[\psi_{20}+\psi_{21}h_1+\psi_{22}h_2+\psi_{23}h_3]\\
h'_3&=a[\psi_{30}+\psi_{31}h_1+\psi_{32}h_2+\psi_{33}h_3]
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Two-layer network

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_1 &= a[\theta_{10}+\theta_{11}x] &
 h'_1 &= a[\psi_{10}+\psi_{11}h_1+\psi_{12}h_2+\psi_{13}h_3]\\
h_2 &= a[\theta_{20}+\theta_{21}x] &
 h'_2 &= a[\psi_{20}+\psi_{21}h_1+\psi_{22}h_2+\psi_{23}h_3]\\
h_3 &= a[\theta_{30}+\theta_{31}x] &
 h'_3 &= a[\psi_{30}+\psi_{31}h_1+\psi_{32}h_2+\psi_{33}h_3]
\end{aligned}
$$

$$y'=\phi'_0+\phi'_1h'_1+\phi'_2h'_2+\phi'_3h'_3$$

![](figures/slide_33_figure_01.png){width="74%"}

---

## Two-layer network as one equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_i &= a[\theta_{i0}+\theta_{i1}x], & i&=1,2,3,\\
h'_i &= a\!\left[\psi_{i0}+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\psi_{ij}h_j\right], & i&=1,2,3,\\
y' &= \phi'_0+\sum_{i=1}^{3}\phi'_i h'_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

Combining the layers:

$$
\boxed{\displaystyle
 y' = \phi'_0+\sum_{i=1}^{3}\phi'_i\,
 a\!\left[\psi_{i0}+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\psi_{ij}
 a(\theta_{j0}+\theta_{j1}x)\right]
}
$$

---

$$y_k=\phi_{k0}+\sum_{i=1}^{4}\phi_{ki}h_i, \quad k=1,2$$

## Networks as composing functions

Consider the *pre-activations* at the second hidden units.

At this point, it is a one-layer network with three outputs.

$$
 h'_i = a\!\left[\underbrace{\psi_{i0}+\sum_{j=1}^3\psi_{ij}h_j}_{\text{pre-activation}}\right], \qquad i=1,2,3
$$

## Hyperparameters

- $K$ layers = **depth** of network
- $D_k$ hidden units per layer = **width** of network

- These are called **hyperparameters** — chosen before training the network.
- Can try retraining with different hyperparameters: **hyperparameter optimization** or **hyperparameter search**.

## Notation change #1 — building matrix notation

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1"}

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_i &= a[\theta_{i0}+\theta_{i1}x],\quad i=1,2,3\\
h'_i &= a[\psi_{i0}+\psi_{i1}h_1+\psi_{i2}h_2+\psi_{i3}h_3],\quad i=1,2,3\\
y' &= \phi'_0+\phi'_1h'_1+\phi'_2h'_2+\phi'_3h'_3
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="2"}

$$
\begin{bmatrix}h_1\\h_2\\h_3\end{bmatrix}
=a\!\left[\begin{bmatrix}\theta_{10}\\\theta_{20}\\\theta_{30}\end{bmatrix}
+\begin{bmatrix}\theta_{11}\\\theta_{21}\\\theta_{31}\end{bmatrix}x\right]
$$

$$h'_i=a\!\left[\psi_{i0}+\sum_{j=1}^3\psi_{ij}h_j\right],\quad i=1,2,3$$

$$y'=\phi'_0+\sum_{i=1}^3\phi'_ih'_i$$

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="3"}

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf h &= a[\boldsymbol\theta_0+\boldsymbol\theta x]\\[3mm]
\begin{bmatrix}h'_1\\h'_2\\h'_3\end{bmatrix}
&= a\!\left[
\begin{bmatrix}\psi_{10}\\\psi_{20}\\\psi_{30}\end{bmatrix}
+\begin{bmatrix}\psi_{11}&\psi_{12}&\psi_{13}\\\psi_{21}&\psi_{22}&\psi_{23}\\\psi_{31}&\psi_{32}&\psi_{33}\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf h\right]
\end{aligned}$$

$$y'=\phi'_0+\sum_{i=1}^3\phi'_ih'_i$$

:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="4"}

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf h &= a[\boldsymbol\theta_0+\boldsymbol\theta x]\\[3mm]
\mathbf h' &= a[\boldsymbol\psi_0+\boldsymbol\Psi\mathbf h]\\[3mm]
y' &= \phi'_0+\begin{bmatrix}\phi'_1&\phi'_2&\phi'_3\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}h'_1\\h'_2\\h'_3\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}$$

:::

:::

---

## Notation change #2

Introduce vectors and matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf h &= a[\boldsymbol\theta_0+\boldsymbol\theta x]\\[2mm]
\mathbf h' &= a[\boldsymbol\psi_0+\boldsymbol\Psi\mathbf h]\\[2mm]
y' &= \phi'_0+\boldsymbol\phi'\mathbf h'
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Notation change #3 — layer indexing

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out data-fragment-index="1"}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf h_1 &= a[\boldsymbol\beta_0+\boldsymbol\Omega_0\mathbf x]\\
\mathbf h_2 &= a[\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\Omega_1\mathbf h_1]\\
\mathbf y &= \boldsymbol\beta_2+\boldsymbol\Omega_2\mathbf h_2
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf h_1 &= a[\underbrace{\boldsymbol\beta_0}_{\text{bias vector}}+
\underbrace{\boldsymbol\Omega_0}_{\text{weight matrix}}\mathbf x]\\
\mathbf h_2 &= a[\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\Omega_1\mathbf h_1]\\
\mathbf y &= \boldsymbol\beta_2+\boldsymbol\Omega_2\mathbf h_2
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

:::

---

## General equations for deep network

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf h_1 &= a[\boldsymbol\beta_0+\boldsymbol\Omega_0\mathbf x]\\
\mathbf h_2 &= a[\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\Omega_1\mathbf h_1]\\
\mathbf h_3 &= a[\boldsymbol\beta_2+\boldsymbol\Omega_2\mathbf h_2]\\
&\,\vdots\\
\mathbf h_K &= a[\boldsymbol\beta_{K-1}+\boldsymbol\Omega_{K-1}\mathbf h_{K-1}]\\
\mathbf y &= \boldsymbol\beta_K+\boldsymbol\Omega_K\mathbf h_K
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, the network computes a composition of affine transformations and activations.

## Shallow vs. deep networks

The best results are created by deep networks with many layers.

- 50–1000 layers for most applications
- Best results in:
    - Computer vision
    - Natural language processing
    - Graph neural networks
    - Generative models
    - Reinforcement learning

All use deep networks. But why?

---

## Shallow vs. deep networks

**1. Ability to approximate different functions?**

Both obey the **universal approximation theorem**.

Argument: One layer is enough, and for deep networks we could arrange for the other layers to compute the identity function.

---

## Shallow vs. deep networks

**2. Number of linear regions per parameter**

---

## Number of linear regions per parameter

![](figures/slide_59_figure_01.png){width="92%"}

- **5 layers; 10 hidden units per layer:** 471 parameters, 161,501 linear regions
- **5 layers; 50 hidden units per layer:** 10,801 parameters, over $10^{40}$ linear regions

---

## Shallow vs. deep networks

**2. Number of linear regions per parameter**

- Deep networks create many more regions per parameter.
- But there are dependencies between them:
    - Think of folding example.
    - Perhaps similar symmetries in real-world functions? **Unknown.**

---

## Shallow vs. Deep Networks

**3. Depth efficiency**

- There are some functions that require a shallow network with **exponentially more hidden units** than a deep network to achieve an equivalent approximation.
- This is known as the **depth efficiency** of deep networks.
- But do the real-world functions we want to approximate have this property? **Unknown.**

---

## Shallow vs. Deep Networks

**4. Large structured networks**

- Think about images as input — might be 1M pixels.
- Fully connected networks are not practical.
- Answer is to have weights that only operate locally, and share across image.
- This leads to **convolutional networks**.
- Gradually integrate information from across the image — needs multiple layers.

---

## Shallow vs. Deep Networks

**5. Fitting and generalization**

- Fitting of deep models seems to be easier up to about 20 layers.
- Then needs various tricks to train deeper networks, so (in vanilla form), fitting becomes harder.
- Generalization is good in deep networks. Why?

---

## Shallow vs. Deep Networks

**5. Fitting and generalization**

Fitting of deep models is also **faster**.

## Where are we going?

- We have defined families of very flexible networks that map multiple inputs to multiple outputs.
- Now we need to train them:
    - How to choose loss functions
    - How to find minima of the loss function
    - How to do this in particular for deep networks
- Then we need to test them.
